claim: Cell cycle tags allow to restrict target protein expression to specific cell cycle phases.
source: Cell cycle tags allow to restrict target protein expression to specific cell cycle phases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of the technology.

claim: The cell cycle tag methodology was initially developed for budding yeast by the Jentsch group (Karras and Jentsch, 2010).
source: The cell cycle tag methodology was initially developed for budding yeast by the Jentsch group (Karras and Jentsch, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Karras and Jentsch, 2010.

claim: The cell cycle tag methodology was expanded by Kolodner and colleagues (Hombauer et al., 2011).
source: expanded by Kolodner and colleagues (Hombauer et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hombauer et al., 2011.

claim: The cell cycle tag methodology was expanded by Kubota and colleagues (Johnson et al., 2016).
source: Kubota and colleagues (Johnson et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2016.

claim: Three cell cycle tags have been developed based on the S phase cyclin Clb6, the M phase cyclin Clb2 and the G1 regulator Sic1 (Karras and Jentsch, 2010; Hombauer et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2016).
source: So far, three cell cycle tags have been developed based on the S phase cyclin Clb6, the M phase cyclin Clb2 and the G1 regulator Sic1 (Karras and Jentsch, 2010; Hombauer et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three papers.

claim: The three cell cycle tags constrain protein expression to S phase, early M phase and late M to G1 phase, respectively.
source: These tags constrain protein expression to S phase, early M phase and late M to G1 phase, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the three tags based on the cyclins they are derived from.

claim: Peak expression levels from the three constructs are vastly different (Sic1 > Clb2 > Clb6).
source: peak expression levels from the three constructs are vastly different (Sic1 > Clb2 > Clb6, compare Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression levels from current cell cycle tag constructs cannot be adjusted, which can lead to under- or overexpression of the protein of interest.
source: expression levels cannot be adjusted, which can lead to under- or overexpression of the protein of interest
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the existing system.

claim: The advanced cell cycle tag toolbox was expanded to 46 constructs.
source: the advanced cell cycle tag toolbox was expanded to 46 constructs
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: New promoters and degrons from Clb5 and Clb1 were used to expand the cell cycle tag toolbox.
source: we used new promoters and degrons from Clb5 and Clb1
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Chimeric promoter-degron combinations were used to expand the cell cycle tag toolbox.
source: chimeric promoter-degron combinations
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Protein expression was crippled using 5´UTR truncations and upstream out of frame ATGs.
source: protein expression was crippled using 5´UTR truncations and upstream out of frame ATGs
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Out-of-frame ATGs reduce protein expression levels by reduced translation rates (Yun et al., 2012; Araujo et al., 2012; Dvir et al., 2013).
source: introduced out-of-frame ATGs, which have been shown to reduce protein expression levels by reduced mRNA stability and reduced translation rates, respectively (Yun et al., 2012; Araujo et al., 2012; Dvir et al., 2013; Merrick and Pavitt, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three papers.

claim: New cell cycle tag constructs allow cell cycle-restricted expression of GFP at varied peak expression levels.
source: New cell cycle tag constructs allow cell cycle-restricted expression of GFP at varied peak expression levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: All constructs restricted protein expression to the target cell cycle phase.
source: Notably, all constructs restricted GFP-expression to the target cell cycle phase (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Constructs containing the Clb6 degron sequence imposed a much sharper restriction of expression to S phase consistent with the differential regulation of Clb5 and Clb6 (Kühne and Linder, 1993; Schwob and Nasmyth, 1993; Jackson et al., 2006).
source: constructs containing the Clb6 degron sequence imposed a much sharper restriction of expression to S phase consistent with the differential regulation of Clb5 and Clb6 (Figure 1B; Kühne and Linder, 1993; Schwob and Nasmyth, 1993; Jackson et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B and citations to three papers.

claim: Within different G1-, S- and M-tag constructs expression varied by up to 10-fold, respectively.
source: This analysis showed that within different G1-, S- and M-tag constructs expression varied by up to 10-fold, respectively (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: M-tag constructs containing the pClb1 promoter or the 5'UTR-truncated pClb2 promoter showed much weaker peak expression levels and tighter temporal restriction of expression.
source: we found that M-tag constructs containing the pClb1 promoter or the 5'UTR-truncated pClb2 promoter showed much weaker peak expression levels and tighter temporal restriction of expression at the same time (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and supplementary figures.

claim: For the G1-tag, upstream out-of-frame ATGs reduced protein expression from pSic1 constructs and led to tighter temporal restriction of expression.
source: Similarly, for the G1-tag we found that upstream out-of-frame ATGs reduced protein expression from pSic1 constructs and also led to tighter temporal restriction of expression (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Clb6pClb6-tagged and Clb2pClb1-tagged versions of Mus81-Mms4 restricted Mus81-Mms4 expression to S and M phase.
source: we found that Clb6pClb6 -80bp-tagged and Clb2pClb1 -150bp-tagged versions of Mus81-Mms4 restricted Mus81-Mms4 expression to S and M phase
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Clb6pClb6 -80bp-tagged and Clb2pClb1 -150bp-tagged versions of Mus81-Mms4 resulted in very similar peak expression levels between 0.9 and 1.2-fold of the endogenous proteins.
source: resulted in very similar peak expression levels between 0.9 and 1.2-fold of the endogenous proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 expression was below endogenous levels in early M phase.
source: we observed that expression of Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 was below endogenous levels in early M phase (see Figure 2B, 37.5 and 45 min time points)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The window of time during which the M phase specific, hyperphosphorylated form of Mms4 was observed was shorter for Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 compared to endogenous Mus81-Mms4.
source: Consistently, the window of time during which we could observe the M phase specific, hyperphosphorylated form of Mms4 was shorter for Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 compared to endogenous Mus81-Mms4 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 and Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 are expressed to very similar levels, but 2 to 5-fold overexpressed compared to endogenous Mus81-Mms4.
source: Comparison of peak expression levels in S and M phase suggests that Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 and Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 are expressed to very similar levels, but 2 to 5-fold overexpressed compared to endogenous Mus81-Mms4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 did not show underexpression in early M phase.
source: when we compared Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 to Mlow-Mus81-Mms4, we noticed that the Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 did neither show underexpression in early M phase (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 did not show a shortened window of M phase-specific Mms4 phosphorylation.
source: nor a shortened window of M phase-specific Mms4 phosphorylation (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: N-terminal tagging does not alter Mus81-Mms4 activity.
source: N-terminal tagging does not alter Mus81-Mms4 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the nHJ cleavage assay shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All versions of Mus81-Mms4 (WT, S-tagged, M-tagged) showed nuclease activity towards a nicked Holliday junction (nHJ) model substrate.
source: we obtained Mus81-Mms4, Clb6 (S-)-tagged Mus81-Mms4 and Clb2 (M-)-tagged Mus81-Mms4 by immuno-purification, phosphatase treated the protein to exclude cell cycle-dependent stimulatory effects and found that all versions showed nuclease activity towards a nicked Holliday junction (nHJ) model substrate (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: mus81Δ cells were hypersensitive to MMS and CPT.
source: mus81Δ cells were hypersensitive to MMS and CPT
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations and data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: mus81Δ cells showed reduced growth on HU containing medium (Xiao et al., 1998; Interthal and Heyer, 2000; Mullen et al., 2001; Bastin-Shanower et al., 2003; Saugar et al., 2013).
source: showed reduced growth on HU containing medium (Figure 3A–B; Xiao et al., 1998; Interthal and Heyer, 2000; Mullen et al., 2001; Bastin-Shanower et al., 2003; Saugar et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A-B and citations to five papers.

claim: Slow-Mus81-Mms4 expressing cells showed similar phenotypes to mus81Δ upon chronic MMS and CPT exposure.
source: Restricting Mus81-Mms4 to S phase also gave a severe hypersensitivity to MMS and CPT: Slow-Mus81-Mms4 expressing cells showed similar phenotypes as mus81Δ (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 showed pronounced hypersensitivity to MMS and CPT, but compared to mus81Δ (and Slow-Mus81-Mms4) the phenotype was less severe.
source: while Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 also showed pronounced hypersensitivity, but compared to mus81Δ (and Slow-Mus81-Mms4) the phenotype was less severe (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 cells did not show any hypersensitivity to MMS and CPT.
source: Specifically, Mhigh-Mus81-Mms4 cells did not show any hypersensitivity (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 cells showed a small but detectable growth defect in the presence of high doses of MMS or CPT.
source: while Mlow-Mus81-Mms4 cells showed a small but detectable growth defect in the presence of high doses of MMS or CPT (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mus81-Mms4 would exhibit its dominant function in the response to genotoxic agents during M phase and not during S phase.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Mus81-Mms4 would exhibit its dominant function in the response to genotoxic agents during M phase and not during S phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic data presented.

claim: Absence of RNaseH1 and RNaseH2 generates replication stress due to defects in the removal of RNA-DNA-hybrids and defects in ribonucleotide excision repair (Sollier and Cimprich, 2015; Hamperl and Cimprich, 2016).
source: Absence of RNaseH1 and RNaseH2 generates replication stress due to defects in the removal of RNA-DNA-hybrids and defects in ribonucleotide excision repair (Sollier and Cimprich, 2015; Hamperl and Cimprich, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two papers.

claim: Mus81 orthologs were first implicated in the replication stress caused by RNaseH-deficiency because of the synthetic growth phenotype of a mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant in S. pombe (Zhao et al., 2018).
source: Mus81 orthologs were first implicated in the replication stress caused by RNaseH-deficiency because of the synthetic growth phenotype of a mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant in S. pombe (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: A similar synthetic growth phenotype is observed in the corresponding budding yeast mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant.
source: We observe a similar synthetic growth phenotype in the corresponding budding yeast mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The synthetic growth phenotype of mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ was further aggravated by addition of HU in low concentrations.
source: which was further aggravated by addition of HU in low concentrations (Figure 3C–D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Presence of M phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 was able to rescue the phenotypes of mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ back to levels of the rnh1Δ rnh201Δ strain.
source: Notably, presence of M phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 was able to rescue these phenotypes back to levels of the rnh1Δ rnh201Δ strain
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C-D.

claim: S phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 were unable to rescue the phenotypes of mus81Δ rnh1Δ rnh201Δ.
source: while S phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 were unable to do so (Figure 3C–D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Single strand breaks generated in the Flp nickase system lead to replication run-off (replication fork breakage) and repair by break-induced replication (BIR) (Nielsen et al., 2009; Mayle et al., 2015).
source: Previous studies have suggested that single strand breaks generated in the Flp nickase system would lead to replication run-off (replication fork breakage) and repair by break-induced replication (BIR) and that Mus81-Mms4 and Yen1 would be redundantly required for survival (Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nielsen et al., 2009 and Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: Mus81-Mms4 and Yen1 are redundantly required for survival in the Flp-nick system (Mayle et al., 2015).
source: that Mus81-Mms4 and Yen1 would be redundantly required for survival (Mayle et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: M phase restriction of Mus81-Mms4 allowed survival similar to WT cells in the Flp-nick system.
source: Notably, however, also in the Flp-nick system, we observed that M phase restriction of Mus81-Mms4 allowed survival similar to WT cells (Figure 3E–F, note the yen1Δ background).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The Slow-Mus81-Mms4 construct led to pronounced sensitivity similar to the MUS81 deletion in the Flp-nick system.
source: In contrast, the Slow-Mus81-Mms4 construct led to pronounced sensitivity similar to the MUS81 deletion
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 led to an intermediary phenotype in the Flp-nick system.
source: while Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 led to an intermediary phenotype (Figure 3E–F)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Restriction of Mus81-Mms4 to S phase renders cells sensitive to various forms of replication stress.
source: Collectively, these data show that restriction of Mus81-Mms4 to S phase renders cells sensitive to various forms of replication stress
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic data presented.

claim: Restriction of Mus81-Mms4 to M phase does not cause a discernible phenotype.
source: while restriction of Mus81-Mms4 to M phase does not cause a discernible phenotype
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic data presented.

claim: In budding yeast the dominant function of Mus81-Mms4 in response to replication stress is post-replicative.
source: suggesting that in budding yeast the dominant function of Mus81-Mms4 in response to replication stress is post-replicative
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic data presented.

claim: Cell cycle restriction of Mus81-Mms4 expression to S or M phase remains intact even after DNA damage induction and recovery.
source: First, we used a single-cell-cycle setup to show that even after DNA damage induction, and recovery, the cell cycle restriction of Mus81-Mms4 expression to S or M phase remains intact (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In budding yeast cyclin-CDK complexes are unlikely to be directly regulated by DNA damage signals (Zegerman and Diffley, 2009).
source: Consistent with the fact that in budding yeast cyclin-CDK complexes are unlikely to be directly regulated by DNA damage signals (Zegerman and Diffley, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2009.

claim: M phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 showed sensitivity similar to WT cells after MMS treatment in S phase.
source: When we next treated cells with MMS in S phase and measured cell survival, we obtained a similar picture as in experiments with chronic exposure: M phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 showed sensitivity similar to WT cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cells expressing S phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 showed hypersensitivity after MMS treatment in S phase, with Slow-Mus81-Mms4 cells similar to the mus81Δ knock-out.
source: In contrast, cells expressing S phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 showed hypersensitivity, with Slow-Mus81-Mms4 cells similar to the mus81Δ knock-out
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 displayed slightly better survival than Slow-Mus81-Mms4 after MMS treatment in S phase.
source: and Shigh-Mus81-Mms4 displaying slightly better survival (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mus81Δ deficiency interferes with recovery of linear chromosomes after MMS treatment in S phase (Ho et al., 2010).
source: Intriguingly, mus81Δ deficiency has been shown to interfere with recovery of linear chromosomes after MMS treatment in S phase (Ho et al., 2010, see Figure 4B–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ho et al., 2010 and data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Cells expressing M phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 versions recover linear chromosomes as WT cells after release from replication fork stalling with MMS in S phase.
source: When we released cells from replication fork stalling with MMS in S phase, we found that cells expressing M phase-restricted Mus81-Mms4 versions recover linear chromosomes as WT cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Cells restricting Mus81-Mms4 to S phase were strongly delayed in the appearance of resolved, linear chromosomes after release from replication fork stalling with MMS in S phase.
source: In contrast, cells restricting Mus81-Mms4 to S phase were strongly delayed in the appearance of resolved, linear chromosomes, as were mus81Δ cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Mus81-Mms4 resolves replication or recombination structures to linear chromosomes in a post-replicative manner during M phase.
source: These data therefore indicate that Mus81-Mms4 resolves replication or recombination structures to linear chromosomes in a post-replicative manner during M phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PFGE data presented.

claim: Cells lacking Mus81-Mms4 showed a strong reduction in the formation of crossover repair products in the DSB-induced recombination assay (Ho et al., 2010).
source: Cells lacking Mus81-Mms4 showed a strong reduction in the formation of crossover repair products (Ho et al., 2010; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ho et al., 2010 and data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells expressing M phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 were proficient in crossover formation as WT cells.
source: Notably, cells expressing M phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 were proficient in crossover formation as WT cells
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: S phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 as well as the MUS81 deletion showed reduced rates of crossover formation.
source: while S phase-restricted versions of Mus81-Mms4 as well as the MUS81 deletion showed reduced rates of crossover formation (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The M phase function of Mus81-Mms4 is linked to its role in forming crossovers.
source: This shows that the M phase function of Mus81-Mms4 is linked to its role in forming crossovers
evidence: This is an inference based on the crossover data presented.

claim: In budding yeast a major function of Mus81-Mms4 is that of a post-replicative resolvase.
source: suggesting that in budding yeast a major function of Mus81-Mms4 is that of a post-replicative resolvase
evidence: This is an inference based on the crossover data presented.

claim: A large proportion of recombination intermediates is typically processed by the Sgs1-Top3-Rmi1 helicase-decatenase complex (Gangloff et al., 1994; Fabre et al., 2002; Wu and Hickson, 2003; Cejka et al., 2010).
source: A large proportion of recombination intermediates is typically processed by the Sgs1-Top3-Rmi1 helicase-decatenase complex (Gangloff et al., 1994; Fabre et al., 2002; Wu and Hickson, 2003; Cejka et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four papers.

claim: A hallmark phenotype of mus81Δ mutants is the synthetic lethality with sgs1Δ (Kaliraman et al., 2001; Mullen et al., 2001; Fabre et al., 2002; Bastin-Shanower et al., 2003).
source: A hallmark phenotype of mus81Δ mutants therefore is the synthetic lethality with sgs1Δ (Kaliraman et al., 2001; Mullen et al., 2001; Fabre et al., 2002; Bastin-Shanower et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four papers.

claim: A strong synthetic phenotype was observed when Mus81 expression was restricted to S phase in the sgs1Δ background.
source: A strong synthetic phenotype was observed when we restricted Mus81 expression to S phase
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: No synthetic defect was seen when Mus81 expression was restricted to M phase in the sgs1Δ background.
source: but no such defect was seen when we restricted Mus81 expression to M phase (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cell cycle tag methodology makes a strong case for Mus81-Mms4 having its dominant function in response to replication perturbation by acting post-replicatively in M phase, likely as a resolvase processing HR or replication intermediates.
source: Overall, the cell cycle tag methodology therefore makes a strong case for Mus81-Mms4 having its dominant function in response to replication perturbation by acting post-replicatively in M phase, likely as a resolvase processing HR or replication intermediates.
evidence: This is an inference based on all the phenotypic data presented.

claim: High levels of resolvase activity during S phase may interfere with replication and the response to replication stalling (Szakal and Branzei, 2013; Blanco et al., 2014; Duda et al., 2016; Pfander and Matos, 2017).
source: We and others have reasoned that high levels of resolvase activity during S phase may interfere with replication and the response to replication stalling (Szakal and Branzei, 2013; Blanco et al., 2014; Duda et al., 2016; Pfander and Matos, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four papers.

claim: Yen1 is cell cycle-controlled and restricted to late M phase by inhibitory cyclin-CDK phosphorylation (Kosugi et al., 2009; Matos et al., 2011; Blanco et al., 2014; Eissler et al., 2014; García-Luis et al., 2014).
source: we turned to a second resolvase – Yen1, which is cell cycle-controlled and restricted to late M phase by inhibitory cyclin-CDK phosphorylation (Kosugi et al., 2009; Matos et al., 2011; Blanco et al., 2014; Eissler et al., 2014; García-Luis et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five papers.

claim: YEN1-ON is deficient in inhibitory CDK phosphorylation sites, constitutively active throughout the cell cycle and detrimental to cellular survival after genotoxic insults as well as during meiosis (Blanco et al., 2014; Eissler et al., 2014; Arter et al., 2018).
source: A mutant version of Yen1 called YEN1-ON is deficient in inhibitory CDK phosphorylation sites, constitutively active throughout the cell cycle and detrimental to cellular survival after genotoxic insults as well as during meiosis (Blanco et al., 2014; Eissler et al., 2014; Arter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three papers.

claim: Clb6pClb6 -80bp-tagged, Clb2pClb2 -60bp-tagged and Sic1pSic1 u(ATA)AUG-tagged versions of Yen1-ON showed peak expression levels in S, M and G1 phase that were between 1.3 to 1.5-fold of Yen1-ON expressed from endogenous promoter.
source: we found that Clb6pClb6 -80bp-tagged, Clb2pClb2 -60bp-tagged and Sic1pSic1 u(ATA)AUG-tagged versions of Yen1-ON showed peak expression levels in S, M and G1 phase that were between 1.3 to 1.5-fold of Yen1-ON expressed from endogenous promoter (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: Clb2pClb1-tagged, Clb6pClb6-tagged and Sic1pSic1 -20bp-tagged versions of Yen1-ON showed 2.5 to 3-fold peak expression levels compared to endogenous Yen1-ON expressed from its endogenous promoter, but similar among the different constructs.
source: Furthermore, Clb2pClb1-tagged, Clb6pClb6-tagged and Sic1pSic1 -20bp-tagged versions of Yen1-ON showed 2.5 to 3-fold peak expression levels compared to endogenous Yen1-ON expressed from its endogenous promoter, but similar among the different constructs (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Only the M phase-restricted version of Yen1-ON and the constitutively expressed Yen1-ON were able to rescue the MMS sensitivity of cells lacking MUS81.
source: Notably, only the M phase-restricted version of Yen1-ON and the constitutively expressed Yen1-ON were able to rescue the MMS sensitivity of cells lacking MUS81
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The S phase-restricted and the G1 phase-restricted versions of Yen1-ON were unable to rescue the MMS sensitivity of cells lacking MUS81.
source: while the S phase-restricted and the G1 phase-restricted versions of Yen1-ON were unable to do so (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Early M phase is a window of opportunity, during which a Mus81-like resolvase must act.
source: These data further indicate that early M phase is a window of opportunity, during which a Mus81-like resolvase must act
evidence: This is an inference based on the Yen1-ON rescue data.

claim: Yen1-ON can take the function of Mus81-Mms4, if specifically activated during early M phase.
source: and that Yen1-ON can take this function, if specifically activated during this time
evidence: This is an inference based on the Yen1-ON rescue data.

claim: YEN1-ON itself induces hypersensitivity towards MMS compared to WT cells (Blanco et al., 2014).
source: Conversely, YEN1-ON itself induces hypersensitivity towards MMS compared to WT cells (Blanco et al., 2014; Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blanco et al., 2014 and data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Restricting Yen1-ON expression to those cell cycle phases where the protein would normally be in its dephosphorylated form is sufficient to suppress the MMS hypersensitivity phenotype.
source: This suggests that restricting Yen1-ON expression to those cell cycle phases where the protein would normally be in its dephosphorylated form is sufficient to suppress the MMS hypersensitivity phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Yen1-ON MMS sensitivity data.

claim: Yen1-ON expression in S or M phase caused MMS hypersensitivity that was similar to what was observed with unrestricted expression of Yen1-ON.
source: In contrast, Yen1-ON expression in S or M phase caused MMS hypersensitivity that was similar to what was observed with unrestricted expression of Yen1-ON (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Yen1-ON phenotypes depend strongly and in a dose-dependent manner on its expression levels (Blanco et al., 2014).
source: Notably, Yen1-ON phenotypes depend strongly and in a dose-dependent manner on its expression levels (Blanco et al., 2014; MG Blanco, personal communication).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blanco et al., 2014 and personal communication.

claim: Shigh-Yen1-ON and Mhigh-Yen1-ON showed slightly increased MMS hypersensitivity compared to Slow-Yen1-ON and Mlow-Yen1-ON.
source: Consistently, we saw slightly increased MMS hypersensitivity in Shigh-Yen1-ON and Mhigh-Yen1-ON compared to Slow-Yen1-ON and Mlow-Yen1-ON (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The presence of deregulated Yen1 in S phase is detrimental to the cellular response to replication stalling.
source: Therefore, we conclude that (i) the presence of deregulated Yen1 in S phase is detrimental to the cellular response to replication stalling
evidence: This is an inference based on the Yen1-ON MMS sensitivity data.

claim: Deregulated Yen1 in M phase is detrimental but can at the same time partially compensate for the absence of Mus81-Mms4.
source: and that (ii) deregulated Yen1 in M phase is detrimental as well but can at the same time partially compensate for the absence of Mus81-Mms4
evidence: This is an inference based on the Yen1-ON rescue and MMS sensitivity data.

claim: The Mms4 subunit of Mus81-Mms4 becomes phosphorylated in M phase (Matos et al., 2011; Gallo-Fernández et al., 2012; Matos et al., 2013; Szakal and Branzei, 2013; Princz et al., 2017).
source: The heterodimeric Mus81-Mms4 nuclease is known to undergo cell cycle regulation with the Mms4 subunit becoming phosphorylated in M phase (Matos et al., 2011; Gallo-Fernández et al., 2012; Matos et al., 2013; Szakal and Branzei, 2013; Princz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five papers.

claim: Mms4 phosphorylation is mediated by the budding yeast cyclin dependent kinase (CDK) Cdk1/Cdc28 and by a complex consisting of two kinases – polo-like kinase Cdc5 and Dbf4-dependent kinase DDK (Cdc7+Dbf4) (Gallo-Fernández et al., 2012; Matos et al., 2013; Szakal and Branzei, 2013; Princz et al., 2017).

claim: Yen1 regulation consists of several layers and involves phosphorylation-dependent inhibition of its catalytic activity as well as phosphorylation-dependent regulation of its sub-cellular localization (Matos et al., 2011; Blanco et al., 2014; Eissler et al., 2014; García-Luis et al., 2014).
